subject: chemistry_2
question_text: NH₃ forms hydrogen bonds, but PH₃ does not. Why?

verification.note: Unit 7 (VA Group Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.83-84, from the shaded sub-box "VA GROUP ELEMENTS" of printed chapter 7 ("7. VA, VIA, VIIA GROUP ELEMENTS & NOBLE GASES"); the book prints this question on book p.83 as VSAQ 6. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK GAP (book p.83, VSAQ 6): the printed answer is one line, "Nitrogen has small size and high electro negativity." It gives no electronegativity values, never explains that hydrogen bonding needs a large electronegativity DIFFERENCE across the E–H bond, and never mentions the consequence the examiner usually wants — the boiling point. All three are added. TREND AND EXCEPTION (this is the classic exception of group 15 and it is stated on the card): boiling points of the hydrides otherwise increase down the group with molar mass, PH₃ < AsH₃ < SbH₃ < BiH₃, but NH₃ does not follow that order — it boils at 239 K, higher than both PH₃ (185 K) and AsH₃ (211 K), because of hydrogen bonding. PH₃ therefore has the LOWEST boiling point in the group, not NH₃. Values are the standard NCERT ones.

steps.why: A hydrogen bond forms between a partly positive H on one molecule and a lone pair on a small electronegative atom of the next. Both halves fail for PH₃: the P–H bond has almost no polarity because P and H have the same electronegativity, and the lone pair on the large P atom is too spread out to attract an H atom.
common_mistakes: Writing that PH₃ has no lone pair, so no hydrogen bond. PH₃ has a lone pair; the P–H bond is the part that is not polar.
Giving only "small size". The electronegativity difference across the N–H bond is the part that is marked.
steps.memory_tip: Hydrogen bonds need N, O or F. Phosphorus is not one of them, and its electronegativity equals that of hydrogen.
steps.margin_note: Quote the two electronegativity values, 3.0 and 2.1. Numbers turn this from a guess into an answer.

steps.why: The boiling point is the measurable result of the hydrogen bonding and is what the examiner usually asks for next. This is the classic exception in group 15: PH₃, not NH₃, has the lowest boiling point of the five hydrides, because the trend from PH₃ downwards follows molar mass while NH₃ is above that order because of hydrogen bonding.
common_mistakes: Writing that NH₃ has the highest boiling point in the group. SbH₃ (255 K) and BiH₃ (290 K) are higher; NH₃ is only higher than PH₃ and AsH₃.
Saying the boiling point falls down the group. From PH₃ onward it rises with molar mass.
steps.memory_tip: PH₃ has the lowest boiling point in group 15, not NH₃. NH₃ is the one that does not follow the order.
steps.margin_note: Two numbers, 239 K and 185 K, plus the word "hydrogen bond", complete this mark.

insider_note: The exception is the part most often written backwards: PH₃ has the LOWEST boiling point in group 15, and NH₃ is above PH₃ and AsH₃ but still below SbH₃ and BiH₃. Write the order PH₃ < AsH₃ < SbH₃ < BiH₃ and then say NH₃ does not follow it.
